title: Earthquakes and resonance
summary: A fault breaks, waves spread out, and a building sways at its own frequency.
cards.0.p: Along a fault, the rocks are locked together by friction, and stress builds up for years. When the strength of the rocks is exceeded, the blocks slip suddenly. The stored energy spreads out as seismic waves.
cards.0.svg#0: Stress builds up on a locked fault
cards.0.svg#2: past its strength the rock slips suddenly: earthquake
cards.0.key: The Earth's crust is made of plates, and the plates move a few cm each year. An earthquake is slowly built-up stress released within seconds.
cards.1.p: The underground point where the break starts is the focus, and the point on the surface directly above it is the epicenter. In most destructive earthquakes the focus is shallow, less than 70 km deep.
cards.1.svg#4: Where the break starts, and the point above it
cards.1.key: In a shallow earthquake the energy reaches the surface with less loss. The location given in the news is the epicenter.
cards.1.once.soru: The news says "the earthquake was 10 km deep." What is 10 km deep?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.yazi: The point where the break started
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: This point is called the focus. The depth is the distance from the surface to the focus.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: Building foundations are only a few meters deep.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: The depth describes the point where the break started.
cards.2.h: Why do earthquakes happen in certain places?
cards.2.p: The Earth's crust is made of slowly moving plates. At their boundaries the plates grind past each other, collide or move apart. Stress builds up on the faults at these boundaries, and most earthquakes happen there.
cards.2.svg#0: Plates grind past each other at a boundary
cards.2.svg#4: schematic; stress builds up along the fault
cards.2.key: About 90% of the world's earthquakes happen in the Ring of Fire around the Pacific. A fault map shows where an earthquake will happen, but it cannot tell when.
cards.2.once.soru: Why are earthquakes frequent in Japan and Chile?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.yazi: They are on a plate boundary
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: Both countries sit on boundaries where plates push against each other. Stress builds up on the faults there.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: Cave collapses cause very small tremors. Large earthquakes happen on faults.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Most large earthquakes come from faults, not volcanoes. Volcanoes form at the same plate boundaries.
cards.3.p: The P wave is longitudinal, arrives first at ≈6 km/s, and passes through every medium. The S wave is transverse, arrives later at ≈3.5 km/s, and cannot pass through liquids.
cards.3.key: The fact that S waves cannot pass through the outer core showed that the outer core is liquid.
cards.4.p: When body waves reach the surface, surface waves form. They are the slowest waves, but their amplitudes are large. Most of the damage to buildings comes from surface waves.
cards.4.svg#3: Seismogram: the three waves arrive in order
cards.4.key: The waves arrive in this order: first P, then S, and last the surface waves.
cards.4.once.soru: In an earthquake there is a slight tremor first, then strong shaking. Which waves cause most of the strong shaking?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: Surface waves arrive last, but their amplitudes are the largest. They shake the ground both sideways and up and down.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: The P wave arrives first. It is the first slight tremor.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: S is stronger than P, but surface waves have a larger amplitude.
cards.5.p: The S wave falls behind the P wave. The time between them (Δt) grows with distance, and each second is about 8 km. Circles drawn by three stations cross at the epicenter.
cards.5.etk.soru: Change the speeds of P and S and the time between them. How does the distance change?
cards.5.key: If Δt = 10 s, the earthquake is about 80 km away. One station gives only the distance.
cards.6.p: Magnitude is a measure of the energy released. When the magnitude goes up by 1, the energy goes up about 32 times. Intensity describes the shaking and damage at one place. It is measured from I to XII and depends on distance and on the ground.
cards.6.key: A magnitude 7 earthquake releases about 1000 times the energy of a magnitude 5.
cards.7.p: A seismograph relies on inertia. A heavy mass hanging from a spring tends to stay where it is, while the frame shakes with the ground. The record of the difference between them is called a seismogram.
cards.7.svg#0: Inertia holds the mass still while the frame shakes
cards.7.svg#3: the difference is recorded; today's devices are electronic
cards.7.key: With a large mass and a soft spring the device is more sensitive. Thousands of stations around the world monitor the ground all the time.
cards.7.once.soru: When a bus starts suddenly, a standing passenger is thrown backward. A seismograph uses the same principle. Which one?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: The heavy mass tends to stay where it is. The difference between it and the frame, which shakes with the ground, is recorded.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: What a seismograph relies on is the tendency of the mass to stay at rest.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: Buoyancy acts in liquids and gases. A seismograph relies on inertia.
cards.8.p: Every building has a natural period, roughly the number of floors times 0.1 s. If the period of the ground shaking comes close to it, the swaying grows. This is called resonance.
cards.8.key: The period of a 10-story building is about 1 s. In resonance, small but well-timed pushes build up a large oscillation. The same thing happens on a swing.
cards.9.p: On loose, wet ground the amplitude of the shaking grows and its period gets longer. This is called site amplification. The ground can also behave like a liquid, which is called liquefaction. In the 1964 Niigata earthquake, apartment buildings tipped over because of liquefaction.
cards.9.key: Long periods put stress on tall buildings. In the same earthquake, damage in two neighboring districts can be very different because of the ground.
cards.10.p: A resistant building needs solid ground, good concrete and proper reinforcement. A seismic isolator separates the building from the ground and lengthens its period. In skyscrapers, a tuned mass damper damps the swaying.
cards.10.key: The terminal of Istanbul's Sabiha Gökçen Airport stands on isolators. The goal is not a building that never sways. It is a building that stays standing without loss of life.
cards.11.p: During the shaking, drop, cover and hold on. That means get down, protect your head and neck, and hold on to something sturdy. Stay away from windows, shelves and elevators. Do not run for the stairs.
cards.11.svg#9: stay away from windows, shelves and elevators
cards.11.svg#10: beforehand: emergency kit, secure your furniture
cards.11.key: Fasten cabinets to the wall ahead of time, prepare an emergency kit, and agree on a meeting place. Preparation is the only real protection.
cards.11.once.soru: You are at home and the shaking starts. What do you do first?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: You get down, protect your head and hold on to something sturdy. That protects you from falling objects.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: You can fall on the stairs during the shaking. Stairs are among the places that take the most damage.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: The glass can break. So stay away from windows.
cards.12.p:
• An earthquake is the sudden release of stress on a fault.
• First P, then S, then the surface waves arrive.
• S waves do not pass through liquids.
• The distance is about 8 km × Δt.
• When the magnitude goes up by 1, the energy goes up about 32 times.
• When the periods are close, there is resonance.
quiz.0.q: Put the waves in the order they arrive at a station (first to arrive on top).
quiz.0.e: The P wave is the fastest (about 6 km/s). The S wave follows it (about 3.5 km/s). Surface waves are the slowest, but their amplitudes are the largest.
quiz.1.q: At a station, 12 s pass between P and S. About how many km away is the earthquake? (Each second ≈ 8 km)
quiz.1.e: The distance is about 8 km × 12 = 96 km. Finding the exact location of the earthquake takes at least three stations.
quiz.2.q: Match the terms with their definitions.
quiz.2.ciftler.0.1: The deep point where the break starts
quiz.2.ciftler.1.1: The surface directly above the focus
quiz.2.ciftler.2.1: A measure of the energy released
quiz.2.ciftler.3.1: Shaking and damage at one place
quiz.2.e: Every earthquake has a single magnitude. Intensity changes from place to place. It is high near the epicenter and on loose ground.
quiz.3.q: In an earthquake, the period of the ground shaking is about 1 s. Which building on the same street is closest to resonance?
quiz.3.e: The natural period is about 0.1 × the number of floors. So the period of the 10-story building is about 1 s. The period of the shaking equals it, so this building sways the most.
quiz.3.y.0: The period of a 3-story building is about 0.3 s. That is far from the 1 s shaking.
quiz.3.y.2: The period of a 20-story building is about 2 s. That is twice the period of the shaking.
quiz.3.y.3: Every building has a different natural period. So buildings respond differently to the shaking.
A:ozet: Release the stress built up on a fault and race the P and S waves to a station. Turn magnitude into energy, and drive buildings into resonance on a shake table.
A:adimlar.0.metin: The two sides of the fault are slowly pushed in opposite directions, but friction keeps the fault locked. Press play and watch the road.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: What happened to the road when the stress exceeded the strength?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: It splits in two, and the pieces stay straight but offset
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The rock slips suddenly and the bend straightens out, but the two sides are now offset. The stored energy spreads out as waves.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The bend in the road is a sign of stress. When the fault breaks, the stress is released and the road straightens.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: It returns to its old straight shape, with no offset
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The blocks really did move during this time. The break completes that slip all at once.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Two kinds of waves, P and S, leave the focus at the same moment. The station is 120 km away.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: Which one reaches the station first?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: P travels at about 6 km/s and S at about 3.5 km/s. Over 120 km, P arrives in 20 s and S in about 34 s.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: S shakes harder, but it is slower.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The two waves leave at the same moment, but their speeds are different. So S falls behind.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Each second of difference between P and S means about 8 km of distance. Place the station where there will be 10 seconds between P and S. Then press play.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.tamam: The distance is about 84 km. The P wave arrives in 14 seconds and the S wave in 24 seconds. Each second of difference is about 8.4 km. That is why the rule is d ≈ 8 km × Δt.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.ipucu: Each 1 second of difference means about 8 km of distance.
A:adimlar.3.metin: When the magnitude goes up by 1, the energy goes up about 32 times. Raise the magnitude. The square stands for the energy released.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: A magnitude 7 earthquake releases about 1000 times (32 × 32) the energy of a magnitude 5. A small difference in magnitude is a huge difference in energy.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.ipucu: Each +1 in magnitude means about 32 times the energy. 32 × 32 is about 1000.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Every building has its own period of oscillation. The table will shake slowly, with a period of 2 s (0.5 Hz). The natural periods of the buildings are written below them.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The period of this building is about 0.3 s. In slow shaking it moves along with the ground and does not bend.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The period of this building is about 1 s, which does not match the 2 s shaking.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The period of this building is about 2 s, equal to that of the shaking. So it goes into resonance. Long-period shaking is dangerous for tall buildings.
A:adimlar.5.metin: A building goes into resonance when the frequency of the shaking equals its own frequency (f = 1/T). Set the frequency, bring the 3-story building into resonance, and press play.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: The period of the 3-story building is ≈ 0.3 s, so f ≈ 3.3 Hz. Short-period shaking on hard ground puts stress on low buildings.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.ipucu: f = 1 / T. The period of the 3-story building is T ≈ 0.1 × 3 = 0.3 s.
A:adimlar.6.metin: The building and the shaking are the same. Play it first without the isolator, then turn the isolator on.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: How does an isolator protect the building?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: It lengthens the building's period, so less shaking gets through
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The flexible bearings absorb the motion of the ground. The building's period moves far from that of the shaking, and resonance is avoided.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: It makes the building stiffer and heavier
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Stiffness shortens the period. An isolator does the opposite and makes the building flexible at its base.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The wave still arrives, and the ground shakes the same way. What changes is how much of the shaking is passed on to the building.
A:kapanis.0: An earthquake is the sudden release of stress built up on a locked fault.
A:kapanis.1: Each second between P and S means about 8 km of distance.
A:kapanis.2: When the magnitude goes up by 1, the energy goes up about 32 times.
A:kapanis.3: If the period of the shaking is close to the building's natural period, there is resonance. An isolator prevents this.
